questions.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨2,2⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(-10,-8)$ and has velocity $⟨0,0⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2,2⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\,\text{d}t,\int 2\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2t+{C}_{1},\,2t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(3)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨2(3)+{C}_{1},\,2(3)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨6+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-6$ and ${C}_{2}=-6.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v(t)=⟨2t-6,\,2t-6⟩.
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-6,\,2t-6⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t,\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{3},\,{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨-10,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨(3)^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{3},\,(3)^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨-10,-8⟩ & =⟨-9+{C}_{3},\,-9+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=-1$ and ${C}_{4}=1.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-6t-1,\,{t}^{2}-6t+1⟩.
$$

questions.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨2t-2,2t⟩\,,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position  $r=⟨-4,-8⟩$ when $t=1,$ find the times when the particle is at the origin.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is at the origin when its position is $r=⟨0,0⟩.$ So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-2,2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-2)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-2t+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-4,\,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨(1)^{2}-2(1)+{C}_{1},\,(1)^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-4,\,-8⟩ & =⟨-1+{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-3$ and ${C}_{2}=-9.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{2}-2t-3,\,{t}^{2}-9⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation $r(t)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =0 \\ ⟨{t}^{2}-2t-3,\,{t}^{2}-9⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-2t-3=(t-3)(t+1) & =0\,⇒\,t=-1,3, \\ {t}^{2}-9=(t+3)(t-3) & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 3.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=3.$

questions.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨12{t}^{2},-{e}^{-t}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(-1,-4)$ and has velocity $⟨0,1⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨12{t}^{2},-{e}^{-t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 12{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\int (-{e}^{-t})\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{3}+{C}_{1},{e}^{-t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨0,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨4({0}^{3})+{C}_{1},{e}^{-0}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,1⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨4{t}^{3},{e}^{-t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨4{t}^{3},{e}^{-t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}+{C}_{3},-{e}^{-t}+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-1,-4⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{4}+{C}_{3},-{e}^{-0}+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,-4⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=-1$ and ${C}_{4}=-3.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{4}-1,-{e}^{-t}-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2{e}^{t}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $r=⟨0,0⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position of $P$ at time $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Do not round the answers.

$r\,(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨${{field-1}},{{field-2}}$⟩$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2{e}^{t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{1},\,2{e}^{t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡0+{C}_{1},\,2{e}^{0}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,2+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-2.$ Therefore, the position vector at time $t$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2{e}^{t}-2⟩.
$$

To find the position vector at time $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we substitute $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the above, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨sin\,(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,2{e}^{\pi /2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2{e}^{\pi /2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2{e}^{\pi /2}-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨6t,\,4t⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position  $r=⟨-12,\,-8⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the times when the particle is at the origin. Do not round the answers.

In **ascending order**, the particle is at the origin when $t=$
{{field-1}}
and $t=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is at the origin when its position is $r=⟨0,0⟩.$ So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨6t,\,4t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 6t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-12,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨3(0)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2(0)^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-12,-8⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have ${C}_{1}=-12$ and ${C}_{2}=-8.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨3{t}^{2}-12,\,2{t}^{2}-8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation $r(t)=⟨0,0⟩.$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨3{t}^{2}-12,\,2{t}^{2}-8⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2}-12 & =3(t-2)(t+2)=0\,⇒\,t=\pm 2, \\ 2{t}^{2}-8 & =2(t-2)(t+2)=0\,⇒\,t=\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, the particle is at the origin when $t=-2$ and $t=2.$
